code.title: Kosaraju SCCs, then count sources and sinks of the condensation
code.python:
import sys
sys.setrecursionlimit(10000)

n = 6
edges = [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 0), (2, 3), (3, 4), (4, 3), (5, 4)]
g = [[] for _ in range(n)]
rg = [[] for _ in range(n)]
for a, b in edges:
    g[a].append(b)
    rg[b].append(a)
print("edges: " + " ".join(f"{a}->{b}" for a, b in edges))

seen = [False] * n
comp = [-1] * n
order = []

def dfs1(v):                 # pass 1: remember the finish order
    seen[v] = True
    for w in g[v]:
        if not seen[w]:
            dfs1(w)
    order.append(v)

def dfs2(v, c):              # pass 2: flood one SCC on the reversed graph
    comp[v] = c
    for w in rg[v]:
        if comp[w] < 0:
            dfs2(w, c)

for v in range(n):
    if not seen[v]:
        dfs1(v)
c = 0                        # latest finisher first: SCC ids come out in topological order
for v in reversed(order):
    if comp[v] < 0:
        dfs2(v, c)
        c += 1

# condensation: only edges that join two different SCCs survive
has_in = [False] * c
has_out = [False] * c
for a, b in edges:
    if comp[a] != comp[b]:
        has_out[comp[a]] = True
        has_in[comp[b]] = True
sources = has_in.count(False)
sinks = has_out.count(False)
print("SCC id of each node: " + " ".join(map(str, comp)))
print("SCC count:", c)
print(f"condensation sources: {sources}, sinks: {sinks}")
# a DAG becomes one big cycle after max(sources, sinks) extra edges
print("edges to add to make it strongly connected:", 0 if c == 1 else max(sources, sinks))
# Time O(V + E), space O(V + E)

followUps:
A condensation always has at least one source and at least one sink, and it can have as many as there are components. It is a DAG, and a walk in a DAG that keeps going backwards (or forwards) must stop somewhere, so a node with no incoming edge and a node with no outgoing edge always exist.

The extremes: if the whole graph is one SCC, the single node is both the only source and the only sink. If there are no edges between components at all, every one of the k components is both a source and a sink. In the program's graph the SCCs are {0,1,2}, {3,4} and {5}; {5} and {0,1,2} are sources, {3,4} is the only sink, so 2 sources and 1 sink, and max(2, 1) = 2 new edges make it strongly connected.

Squash every SCC into one node, give it a weight equal to its size, and take the heaviest path in the resulting DAG. Inside an SCC you can walk around and visit all of its nodes before leaving, so each component counts in full.

  1. Find SCCs and size[c].
  2. Go through components in topological order.
  3. best[c] = size[c] + the largest best of a component with an edge into c.
for (int c : topoOrder) {
  best[c] += size[c];
  for (int d : dag[c]) best[d] = Math.max(best[d], best[c]);
  ans = Math.max(ans, best[c]);
}

Example: components of sizes 3 → 2 and 1 → 2 give best = 3 + 2 = 5. Time and space are O(V + E).

code.title: Tarjan SCC: one DFS, components pop out in reverse topological order
code.python:
import sys
sys.setrecursionlimit(10000)

n = 8
edges = [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 0), (2, 3), (3, 4), (4, 5), (5, 3), (6, 5), (6, 7), (7, 6)]
g = [[] for _ in range(n)]
for a, b in edges:
    g[a].append(b)
print("edges: " + " ".join(f"{a}->{b}" for a, b in edges))

disc = [-1] * n
low = [0] * n
on_stack = [False] * n
stack = []
timer = 0
count = 0

def dfs(v):
    global timer, count
    disc[v] = low[v] = timer             # visit time; low starts equal to it
    timer += 1
    stack.append(v)
    on_stack[v] = True
    for w in g[v]:
        if disc[w] < 0:
            dfs(w)
            low[v] = min(low[v], low[w])
        elif on_stack[w]:                # edge back into the open part
            low[v] = min(low[v], disc[w])
    if low[v] == disc[v]:                # v is the root of an SCC: pop it off the stack
        members = []
        while True:
            w = stack.pop()
            on_stack[w] = False
            members.append(w)
            if w == v:
                break
        print(f"SCC {count}: " + " ".join(map(str, members)))
        count += 1

# one DFS pass, no reversed graph; SCCs come out in reverse topological order
for v in range(n):
    if disc[v] < 0:
        dfs(v)
print("SCC count:", count)
# Time O(V + E), space O(V)

followUps:
Kosaraju is the easier one to write without recursion. Its second pass only has to collect everything reachable in the reversed graph, so any plain traversal works there, even a BFS with a queue. Only the first pass needs the finish order, and that takes one explicit stack plus a "next edge" index per vertex.

Tarjan is harder because it does work after a child returns: low[v] = min(low[v], low[child]) and the pop of a finished component. In an iterative version you must do that work at the moment you pop the child from your own stack, and forgetting it is the usual bug. Example: on a chain of 200,000 nodes both run in O(V + E) time with O(V) heap memory, but the Kosaraju loop is about half as long.

You need the topological order of the condensation: a variable is set to true when its own component comes later in that order than the component of its negation. Later means "nothing forces anything after it", so the choice cannot cause a contradiction further down.

How this looks depends on the algorithm. Kosaraju numbers components in topological order, so the rule is x = comp[x] > comp[¬x]. Tarjan finishes sink components first, so its numbers are in reverse topological order and the rule flips to comp[x] < comp[¬x].

Tiny check: the clause (x ∨ x) gives the edge ¬x → x. ¬x is earlier, x is later, so x = true, which is correct. Picking the other way round would set x = false and break the clause.

code.title: Bridges and articulation points with disc and low
code.python:
import sys
sys.setrecursionlimit(10000)

n = 7
eu = [0, 1, 2, 1, 3, 4, 5, 5]
ev = [1, 2, 0, 3, 4, 5, 3, 6]
adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]            # adj[v] = ids of edges touching v
for i in range(len(eu)):
    adj[eu[i]].append(i)
    adj[ev[i]].append(i)
print("edges: " + " ".join(f"{a}-{b}" for a, b in zip(eu, ev)))

disc = [-1] * n
low = [0] * n
is_ap = [False] * n
bridges = []
timer = 0

def dfs(v, parent_edge):
    global timer
    disc[v] = low[v] = timer
    timer += 1
    children = 0
    for i in adj[v]:
        if i == parent_edge:             # skip only the edge we came by
            continue
        w = eu[i] ^ ev[i] ^ v            # the other end of edge i
        if disc[w] >= 0:                 # back edge
            low[v] = min(low[v], disc[w])
            continue
        children += 1
        dfs(w, i)
        low[v] = min(low[v], low[w])
        if low[w] > disc[v]:             # subtree cannot reach v
            bridges.append(f"{eu[i]}-{ev[i]}")
        if parent_edge != -1 and low[w] >= disc[v]:   # subtree cannot get above v
            is_ap[v] = True
    if parent_edge == -1 and children >= 2:           # root rule
        is_ap[v] = True

for v in range(n):
    if disc[v] < 0:
        dfs(v, -1)
print("disc: " + " ".join(map(str, disc)))
print("low:  " + " ".join(map(str, low)))
print("bridges: " + " ".join(bridges))
print("articulation points: " + " ".join(str(v) for v in range(n) if is_ap[v]))
# Time O(V + E), space O(V + E)

followUps:
The root needs its own rule because the normal test is always true for it. The root has the smallest disc (0), so low[w] ≥ disc[root] holds for every child and the root would be reported in every graph.

The normal test asks "can this child's subtree reach something above v?". The root has nothing above it, so the only way it can separate the graph is by separating its own subtrees from each other. In an undirected DFS there are no edges between two different child subtrees, so two or more DFS children means removing the root disconnects them.

Example: path 0 – 1 – 2. Started at 0, the root has one child, so it is not an articulation point. Started at 1, the root has two children (0 and 2), so it is one.

Only the bridge code changes: you must skip the one edge id you arrived by, not every edge that leads to the parent vertex. With two edges A–B, the second one is a real way back to A, so it must be seen as a back edge and lower low[B] to disc[A]; then low[B] > disc[A] is false and no bridge is reported.

So a doubled edge is never a bridge, and you need adjacency lists that store (neighbour, edge id). Articulation points do not change at all: removing a vertex removes all of its edges at once, so the number of parallel edges does not matter. Self-loops can be ignored for both. The cost stays O(V + E).

Keep a stack of edges during the same DFS and cut it each time the articulation test fires. A biconnected component is a maximal set of edges that stays connected when any one vertex is removed.

  1. Push every edge when you first walk it (tree edge, or back edge to an ancestor).
  2. After child w returns, if low[w] ≥ disc[v], pop edges until you have popped (v, w). The popped edges are one component.
edgeStack.push(id); dfs(w, id);
low[v] = Math.min(low[v], low[w]);
if (low[w] >= disc[v]) {
  do { e = edgeStack.pop(); comp[e] = count; } while (e != id);
  count++;
}

The program's graph gives 4 components: triangle 0-1-2, bridge 1-3, triangle 3-4-5, bridge 5-6. Time and space O(V + E).

code.title: Parallel edges: skipping the parent vertex versus the parent edge id
code.python:
import sys
sys.setrecursionlimit(10000)

n = 3
eu = [0, 0, 1]                      # two cables 0-1, one cable 1-2
ev = [1, 1, 2]
adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
for i in range(len(eu)):
    adj[eu[i]].append(i)
    adj[ev[i]].append(i)

def bridges(skip_vertex):
    # skip_vertex = True is the buggy version; False skips only the arrival edge id
    disc = [-1] * n
    low = [0] * n
    out = []
    timer = [0]

    def dfs(v, parent, parent_edge):
        disc[v] = low[v] = timer[0]
        timer[0] += 1
        for i in adj[v]:
            w = eu[i] ^ ev[i] ^ v
            if (w == parent) if skip_vertex else (i == parent_edge):
                continue
            if disc[w] >= 0:                 # second cable lands here
                low[v] = min(low[v], disc[w])
                continue
            dfs(w, v, i)
            low[v] = min(low[v], low[w])
            if low[w] > disc[v]:
                out.append(f" {eu[i]}-{ev[i]}(edge {i})")

    for v in range(n):
        if disc[v] < 0:
            dfs(v, -1, -1)
    return "".join(out)

print("cables: 0-1(edge 0) 0-1(edge 1) 1-2(edge 2)")
print("skip parent VERTEX (bug):" + bridges(True))
print("skip parent EDGE id (fix):" + bridges(False))
# Time O(V + E), space O(V + E) for both versions

followUps:
I would give every edge a number and store edge ids in the adjacency lists. Two flat arrays hold the ends of each edge, and each vertex keeps the list of ids that touch it, so two cables between the same routers are simply two different ids.

int[] eu, ev;                 // ends of edge id
List<Integer>[] adj;          // adj[v] = edge ids
adj[eu[id]].add(id); adj[ev[id]].add(id);
int w = eu[id] ^ ev[id] ^ v;  // other end of the edge
if (id == parentEdge) continue;

Example: cables 0–1, 0–1, 1–2 become ids 0, 1, 2 and adj[1] = [0, 1, 2]. Arriving at 1 by id 0, the DFS skips only id 0 and still sees id 1 as a back edge to router 0. Memory is O(V + E), and the reported bridges can be printed by id.

No. SCC algorithms work on directed graphs and never skip a "parent", so there is nothing to get wrong. In an undirected graph the edge back to the parent is the same edge you just used, which is why it must be ignored. In a directed graph an edge v → u back to the vertex you came from is a different, real edge, and it closes a real cycle.

Example: edges 0 → 1 and 1 → 0. Tarjan visits 0, then 1, sees 1 → 0 with 0 still on the stack, sets low[1] = disc[0] and correctly reports one SCC {0, 1}. Two parallel edges 0 → 1 change nothing: the second one is just looked at twice. The check that matters in Tarjan is onStack[w], not who the parent is.

code.title: Hierholzer: Euler path in a directed graph
code.python:
n = 5
edges = [(0, 3), (3, 4), (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 0)]
g = [[] for _ in range(n)]
diff = [0] * n                       # out-degree minus in-degree
for a, b in edges:
    g[a].append(b)
    diff[a] += 1
    diff[b] -= 1
print("edges: " + " ".join(f"{a}->{b}" for a, b in edges))

# degree test: at most one start (out - in = 1) and one end (in - out = 1)
start, plus, minus, ok = edges[0][0], 0, 0, True
for v in range(n):
    if diff[v] == 1:
        plus += 1
        start = v
    elif diff[v] == -1:
        minus += 1
    elif diff[v] != 0:
        ok = False
ok = ok and plus == minus and plus <= 1
print(f"degree test passed: {'yes' if ok else 'no'}, start = {start}")

nxt = [0] * n                        # next unused edge of each vertex
stack = [start]
path = []
while stack:
    v = stack[-1]
    if nxt[v] < len(g[v]):           # walk an unused edge
        stack.append(g[v][nxt[v]])
        nxt[v] += 1
    else:                            # stuck: v is final, written back to front
        path.append(stack.pop())
path.reverse()
print("Euler path: " + " ".join(map(str, path)))
# fewer than E + 1 vertices means some edges were in another piece
print("uses every edge: " + ("yes" if ok and len(path) == len(edges) + 1 else "no"))
# Time O(V + E), space O(V + E)

followUps:
Sort each vertex's outgoing edges and always take the smallest unused one; Hierholzer's back-to-front writing then gives the smallest valid path. You still need the "pop when stuck" step, because plain greedy can walk into a dead end too early.

Example (Reconstruct Itinerary): JFK → KUL, JFK → NRT, NRT → JFK. Greedy takes KUL first and is stuck with two tickets unused. Hierholzer also goes to KUL first, gets stuck, writes KUL as the last stop, then walks JFK → NRT → JFK. Reversed result: JFK, NRT, JFK, KUL, the smallest route that uses every ticket.

In practice sort each list in descending order and pop from the end, or use a min-heap per vertex. Sorting costs O(E log E); the walk itself is still O(V + E).

A de Bruijn sequence is an Euler circuit written down. It is a cyclic string in which every possible word of length n over k symbols appears exactly once.

Build a graph whose nodes are all words of length n − 1. From each node add one edge per symbol: appending the symbol and dropping the first letter gives the next node, and the edge stands for the word of length n. Every node has k edges in and k edges out, so an Euler circuit exists. Walk it with Hierholzer and write one symbol per edge.

Example with k = 2, n = 2: nodes 0 and 1, edges 00, 01, 11, 10. The circuit gives 0011, and read as a circle it contains 00, 01, 11 and 10 once each. The length is kn, and the time is O(kn).

The Chinese Postman problem asks for the shortest closed walk that uses every edge at least once, like a postman who must walk every street and return home.

If every vertex has even degree, an Euler circuit exists and the answer is simply the sum of all edge weights. Otherwise some edges must be walked twice. The odd-degree vertices always come in an even number: pair them up so that the total shortest-path distance between partners is as small as possible, duplicate the edges on those paths, and now all degrees are even, so take an Euler circuit.

Example: path A – B – C with weights 3 and 4. A and C are odd, their distance is 7, so the answer is 7 + 7 = 14. Cost: shortest paths between the odd vertices plus a minimum-weight perfect matching (a bitmask DP of O(2k·k) works for up to about 20 odd vertices).

code.title: Binary lifting: LCA and distance queries on a tree
code.python:
LOG = 4                                   # 2^4 = 16 > 9 nodes
parent = [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 4, 4, 7]      # parent[v] < v; the root 0 points to itself
n = len(parent)
depth = [0] * n
for v in range(1, n):
    depth[v] = depth[parent[v]] + 1
up = [parent[:]]
for k in range(1, LOG):                   # 2^k-th ancestor = two jumps of 2^(k-1)
    up.append([up[k - 1][up[k - 1][v]] for v in range(n)])
print("parent: " + " ".join(map(str, parent)))

def lca(u, v):
    if depth[u] < depth[v]:
        u, v = v, u
    diff = depth[u] - depth[v]
    for k in range(LOG):                  # lift the deeper node to the same depth
        if diff >> k & 1:
            u = up[k][u]
    if u == v:
        return u
    for k in range(LOG - 1, -1, -1):      # jump both while the ancestors still differ
        if up[k][u] != up[k][v]:
            u, v = up[k][u], up[k][v]
    return up[0][u]                       # one step below the LCA

for a, b in [(3, 6), (6, 8), (5, 8), (7, 8)]:
    c = lca(a, b)
    dist = depth[a] + depth[b] - 2 * depth[c]
    print(f"lca({a}, {b}) = {c}, distance = {dist}")
# Build O(N log N) time and space; each query O(log N)

followUps:
About 80 MB for the jump table. You need LOG = 20 levels because 220 = 1,048,576 is the first power of two above 106, and each level holds one 4-byte int per node: 20 × 106 × 4 bytes = 80 MB, plus 4 MB for the depth array.

That fits a 256 MB limit in Java or C++ if you use flat int arrays. A Python list of lists costs at least 8 bytes per entry, so 160 MB or more, which usually does not fit.

If memory is tight: the Euler tour with a sparse table is larger still (about 2N entries × 21 levels), so prefer methods with O(N) memory, such as Tarjan's offline LCA when all queries are known, or heavy-light decomposition, which answers each query in O(log N).

Add the two depths and subtract twice the depth of their LCA: dist(u, v) = depth[u] + depth[v] − 2·depth[lca(u, v)]. The path from u to v goes up to the LCA and then down, and the part from the root to the LCA is counted in both depths, so it is removed twice.

Example from the program: nodes 5 and 8 have depths 2 and 4 and their LCA is the root with depth 0, so the distance is 2 + 4 − 0 = 6 edges. Nodes 6 and 8: depths 3 and 4, LCA 4 at depth 2, distance 3 + 4 − 4 = 3.

For weighted edges store distRoot[v], the sum of weights from the root, and use the same formula with it. Each query costs one LCA: O(log N) with binary lifting, after an O(N log N) build.

code.title: Max flow with and without reverse edges (4 versus 5)
code.python:
N = 4                                         # 0 = S, 1 = A, 2 = B, 3 = T
INF = float("inf")

def max_flow(use_reverse):
    cap = [[0, 3, 2, 0], [0, 0, 2, 2], [0, 0, 0, 3], [0, 0, 0, 0]]

    # push up to 'limit' units from u to T along edges that still have room
    def dfs(u, limit, seen):
        if u == N - 1:
            return limit
        seen[u] = True
        for v in range(N):
            if seen[v] or cap[u][v] == 0:
                continue
            pushed = dfs(v, min(limit, cap[u][v]), seen)
            if pushed > 0:
                cap[u][v] -= pushed               # forward residual shrinks
                if use_reverse:
                    cap[v][u] += pushed           # reverse edge: permission to undo
                return pushed
        return 0

    total = 0
    while True:
        pushed = dfs(0, INF, [False] * N)
        if pushed == 0:
            break
        print("  augment by", pushed)
        total += pushed
    return total

print("network: S->A:3 S->B:2 A->B:2 A->T:2 B->T:3")
print("without reverse edges:")
print("  flow =", max_flow(False))                # greedy gets stuck at 4
print("with reverse edges:")
print("  flow =", max_flow(True))                 # can undo A->B and reach 5
# Ford-Fulkerson with DFS: O(E * F) time (F = flow value), O(V^2) space for the matrix

followUps:
The final flow is S→A 3, S→B 2, A→B 1, A→T 2, B→T 3, for a total of 5.

Check that nothing is lost at the middle nodes: A receives 3 and sends 1 + 2 = 3; B receives 2 + 1 = 3 and sends 3. Out of S goes 3 + 2 = 5 and into T comes 2 + 3 = 5.

The interesting edge is A→B. The first path put 2 units on it; the path through the reverse edge B→A cancelled 1 of them, leaving 1. Nothing was really sent "backwards": one unit that used to go A→B→T now goes A→T, and B→T carries a unit from S→B instead.

Both edges out of S are full, so the cut {S} | {A, B, T} has capacity 3 + 2 = 5, which proves that 5 is the maximum.

Add edges in pairs to one array, so the forward edge gets an even index and its reverse the next odd index; then the partner of edge id is id ^ 1. No searching is needed.

void addEdge(int u, int v, int c) {
  adj[u].add(to.size()); to.add(v); cap.add(c);   // id = 2k
  adj[v].add(to.size()); to.add(u); cap.add(0);   // id = 2k + 1
}
// push f along edge id:
cap[id] -= f; cap[id ^ 1] += f;

Example: the first edge S→A gets id 0 and its reverse A→S gets id 1; 0 ^ 1 = 1 and 1 ^ 1 = 0. The other common way is to store in each edge object the position of its reverse in the neighbour's list (rev). With a capacity matrix the reverse of cap[u][v] is simply cap[v][u], at O(V²) memory.

code.title: Max flow, then read the min cut from the residual graph
code.python:
from collections import deque

def bfs(res, s):
    # BFS over edges with residual > 0; returns parent[] (-1 = not reached)
    n = len(res)
    par = [-1] * n
    par[s] = s
    q = deque([s])
    while q:
        u = q.popleft()
        for v in range(n):
            if par[v] < 0 and res[u][v] > 0:
                par[v] = u
                q.append(v)
    return par

cap = [[0, 4, 3, 0], [0, 0, 2, 1], [0, 0, 0, 6], [0, 0, 0, 0]]
n, s, t, flow = 4, 0, 3, 0
res = [row[:] for row in cap]
print("edges: 0->1:4 0->2:3 1->2:2 1->3:1 2->3:6, S = 0, T = 3")
while True:                                   # Edmonds-Karp
    par = bfs(res, s)
    if par[t] < 0:
        break
    push = float("inf")
    v = t
    while v != s:
        push = min(push, res[par[v]][v])
        v = par[v]
    v = t
    while v != s:
        res[par[v]][v] -= push
        res[v][par[v]] += push
        v = par[v]
    flow += push
print("max flow =", flow)
side = bfs(res, s)                            # what S can still reach = S side of the cut
print("S side: " + " ".join(str(v) for v in range(n) if side[v] >= 0))
cut = 0
# cut edges: original edges from a reached node to an unreached node (all full)
for u in range(n):
    for v in range(n):
        if side[u] >= 0 and side[v] < 0 and cap[u][v] > 0:
            print(f"cut edge {u}->{v} capacity {cap[u][v]}")
            cut += cap[u][v]
print(f"cut capacity = {cut} (equals the max flow)")
# Edmonds-Karp O(V * E^2) time; cut extraction one BFS; O(V^2) space for the matrix

followUps:
No. The value of the minimum cut is unique, but several different sets of edges can have that value.

Example: S → A → T with both capacities 1. The max flow is 1, and both {S→A} and {A→T} are minimum cuts.

The BFS from S in the residual graph gives the minimum cut closest to S. A second search, backwards from T over residual edges, gives the nodes that can still reach T and so the minimum cut closest to T. The minimum cut is unique exactly when these two answers are the same split, that is, when every node is either reachable from S or able to reach T. In the example A is neither, which is why there are two cuts. Both searches cost O(V + E) after the flow is computed.

An edge u → v is in every minimum cut exactly when, in the final residual graph, u is reachable from S and v can reach T. Such an edge is the only thing stopping one more unit of flow, so raising its capacity would raise the max flow, and every minimum cut must contain it.

  1. Compute a max flow.
  2. BFS from S over residual edges: mark fromS.
  3. BFS from T over residual edges walked backwards: mark toT.
  4. Report edges with fromS[u] && toT[v].

Example: S → A (cap 1), A → T (cap 2). S is reachable from S, and A still reaches T with residual 1, so S→A is in every min cut. If both capacities are 1, A cannot reach T and is not reachable from S, so neither edge is in every min cut. The extra work is O(V + E).

Use the Stoer–Wagner algorithm for an undirected weighted graph; it finds the global minimum cut in O(V³) with a matrix (or O(V·E + V² log V) with a heap) and needs no flow at all.

It runs V − 1 phases. In each phase, start anywhere and keep adding the vertex most strongly connected to the set built so far. Call the last two vertices added s and t. The total weight of t's edges is the "cut of the phase", a minimum s–t cut. Record it, merge s and t into one vertex, and repeat. The smallest recorded value is the answer.

Alternatives: fix one vertex as S and run a max flow to each of the other V − 1 vertices (simple, but V − 1 flows), or Karger's random edge contraction, which is fast and simple but only correct with high probability after many repeats.

code.title: Dinic: level graph and blocking flow, phase by phase
code.python:
from collections import deque

n, s, t = 6, 0, 5
to, cap = [], []
adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]

def add_edge(u, v, c):                  # edge id and id ^ 1 are a forward/reverse pair
    adj[u].append(len(to)); to.append(v); cap.append(c)
    adj[v].append(len(to)); to.append(u); cap.append(0)

def bfs():                              # level = BFS distance from S in the residual graph
    level = [-1] * n
    level[s] = 0
    q = deque([s])
    while q:
        u = q.popleft()
        for i in adj[u]:
            if cap[i] > 0 and level[to[i]] < 0:
                level[to[i]] = level[u] + 1
                q.append(to[i])
    return level

def dfs(u, limit):                      # only walk edges that go one level deeper
    if u == t:
        return limit
    while it[u] < len(adj[u]):          # current-edge pointer: never retry a dead edge
        i = adj[u][it[u]]
        v = to[i]
        if cap[i] > 0 and level[v] == level[u] + 1:
            pushed = dfs(v, min(limit, cap[i]))
            if pushed > 0:
                cap[i] -= pushed
                cap[i ^ 1] += pushed
                return pushed
        it[u] += 1
    return 0

edges = [(0, 1, 16), (0, 2, 13), (1, 2, 10), (2, 1, 4), (1, 3, 12), (3, 2, 9), (2, 4, 14), (4, 3, 7), (3, 5, 20), (4, 5, 4)]
for u, v, c in edges:
    add_edge(u, v, c)
print("edges: " + " ".join(f"{u}->{v}:{c}" for u, v, c in edges))
flow = phases = 0
while True:                             # one phase = one level graph + one blocking flow
    level = bfs()
    if level[t] < 0:
        break
    it = [0] * n
    phase_flow = 0
    while True:
        pushed = dfs(s, float("inf"))
        if pushed == 0:
            break
        phase_flow += pushed
    flow += phase_flow
    phases += 1
    print(f"phase {phases}: distance S-T = {level[t]}, pushed {phase_flow}")
print("max flow =", flow)
# Dinic: O(V^2 * E) time in general, O(V + E) space

followUps:
Because a blocking flow destroys every shortest path, and the only new residual edges it creates point backwards in the level graph, so they cannot build a new path of the same length.

Let d be the S–T distance in this phase. The phase ends when every path of length d in the level graph has a full edge. Pushing flow along an edge from level i to level i + 1 adds its reverse, which goes from level i + 1 back to i. A path that uses such an edge loses a level instead of gaining one, so it needs at least d + 2 edges. Old edges that were not in the level graph never go forward by more than one level. So no path of length d is left and the next distance is at least d + 1.

The distance is at most V − 1, so there are at most V − 1 phases. In the program the distance goes from 3 to 4 and then T is unreachable.

It prevents looking at the same useless edge again and again inside one phase. it[u] remembers the first edge of u that might still work; edges before it are skipped for the rest of the phase.

This is safe because levels do not change during a phase: once an edge is full, or leads to a node that cannot reach T in the level graph, it stays useless until the next BFS.

Example: node u has 1,000 dead-end edges followed by one good edge, and 1,000 paths go through u. Without the pointer each of the 1,000 searches rescans the 1,000 dead edges: about 1,000,000 steps. With it the dead edges are scanned once: about 2,000 steps.

It is what gives the O(V·E) bound for one blocking flow and so O(V²·E) overall; without it Dinic can become far slower on dense graphs.

code.title: Doctor holiday scheduling as a max-flow network
code.python:
from collections import deque

def max_flow(res, s, t):                      # Edmonds-Karp on a capacity matrix
    n, flow = len(res), 0
    while True:
        par = [-1] * n
        par[s] = s
        q = deque([s])
        while q:
            u = q.popleft()
            for v in range(n):
                if par[v] < 0 and res[u][v] > 0:
                    par[v] = u
                    q.append(v)
        if par[t] < 0:
            return flow
        push, v = float("inf"), t
        while v != s:
            push = min(push, res[par[v]][v])
            v = par[v]
        v = t
        while v != s:
            res[par[v]][v] -= push
            res[v][par[v]] += push
            v = par[v]
        flow += push

D, P, DAYS = 3, 2, 4                          # days 0,1 = period 0; days 2,3 = period 1
max_shifts = [2, 2, 1]
avail = [[0, 1, 2], [1, 3], [0, 3]]           # days each doctor can work
S, T = 0, 1 + D + D * P + DAYS
cap = [[0] * (T + 1) for _ in range(T + 1)]
for d in range(D):
    cap[S][1 + d] = max_shifts[d]             # S -> doctor: total shifts
    for p in range(P):
        cap[1 + d][1 + D + d * P + p] = 1     # one shift per period
    for x in avail[d]:
        cap[1 + D + d * P + x // 2][1 + D + D * P + x] = 1   # only available days
    print(f"doctor {d}: max {max_shifts[d]} shifts, available [" + ", ".join(map(str, avail[d])) + "]")
for x in range(DAYS):
    cap[1 + D + D * P + x][T] = 1             # each day needs one doctor
flow = max_flow(cap, S, T)
print(f"max flow = {flow} of {DAYS} days -> " + ("feasible" if flow == DAYS else "not feasible"))
# a used (doctor, period) -> day edge shows up as residual 1 on the reverse edge
for x in range(DAYS):
    for d in range(D):
        if cap[1 + D + D * P + x][1 + D + d * P + x // 2] == 1:
            print(f"day {x} -> doctor {d}")
# Nodes: 2 + D + D*P + days; Edmonds-Karp O(V * E^2) time, O(V^2) space

followUps:
Give the edge S → doctor a lower bound as well as a capacity, and turn the problem into a plain max flow with an extra source and sink that force the required units through.

  1. For an edge u → v that must carry between lo and hi: keep it with capacity hi − lo.
  2. Add S' → v with capacity lo and u → T' with capacity lo.
  3. Add T → S with infinite capacity so flow can circulate.
  4. Run max flow from S' to T'. A schedule exists only if every edge out of S' is full.

Example: doctor B must work at least 1 and at most 2 shifts. S → B gets capacity 2 − 1 = 1, plus S' → B with 1 and S → T' with 1. If the flow from S' is less than the sum of all lower bounds, some doctor cannot reach their minimum. To also cover every day, give each day → T edge lo = hi = 1. Cost: one max flow on a graph with two extra nodes.

Put a price on each doctor's edge and ask for the cheapest flow of the required size instead of just any flow. The edge S → doctor d gets cost rate[d] per unit; all other edges cost 0. Then find a minimum-cost flow whose value equals the number of days.

The usual method is successive shortest paths: repeatedly find the cheapest augmenting path by cost (Bellman-Ford or SPFA, or Dijkstra with potentials) and push along it. A reverse edge has the negative cost, so undoing a choice refunds its price.

Example: day 1 can be covered by doctor A at 100 or doctor B at 80, and both have a free shift. The first cheapest path goes through B, cost 80. If B is later needed for a day only B can cover, a path through the reverse edge moves day 1 to A.

Cost: one shortest-path search per unit of flow, about O(days · E log V).

code.title: Kuhn bipartite matching and the König numbers
code.python:
adj = [[0, 1], [0], [1, 2], [2]]     # adj[left] = right vertices it likes
L, R = len(adj), 4
match_r = [-1] * R                   # match_r[r] = left partner of r, or -1

def try_kuhn(u, seen):
    # try to give left vertex u a partner; may push earlier owners to another choice
    for r in adj[u]:
        if seen[r]:
            continue
        seen[r] = True               # ask each right vertex once per round
        if match_r[r] < 0 or try_kuhn(match_r[r], seen):   # r is free, or its owner can move
            match_r[r] = u
            return True
    return False

size = 0
for u in range(L):
    print(f"L{u} likes [" + ", ".join(map(str, adj[u])) + "]")
    if try_kuhn(u, [False] * R):     # fresh marks for every left vertex
        size += 1
print("pairs: " + " ".join(f"L{match_r[r]}-R{r}" for r in range(R) if match_r[r] >= 0))
print("maximum matching =", size)
# Konig (bipartite only): min vertex cover = matching, max independent set = V - matching
print("minimum vertex cover =", size)
print("maximum independent set =", L + R - size)
# Time O(V * E), space O(V + E)

followUps:
Start from the unmatched left vertices, walk alternating paths, and then take the left vertices you did not reach plus the right vertices you did reach.

  1. Mark every unmatched left vertex.
  2. From a marked left vertex go to right neighbours over edges that are not in the matching; from a marked right vertex go to its matched partner.
  3. Cover = unmarked left + marked right.

Example from the program (pairs L1–R0, L0–R1, L2–R2; L3 unmatched): L3 → R2 → L2 → R1 → L0 → R0 → L1. Every left vertex is marked, and R0, R1, R2 are marked. Cover = {R0, R1, R2}, size 3 = the matching size, and every edge does touch one of them.

It is one BFS or DFS after the matching: O(V + E).

Both need different algorithms, and König's theorem no longer holds for general graphs.

Weighted bipartite (the assignment problem): maximise or minimise total weight rather than the number of pairs. Use the Hungarian algorithm, O(n³), or model it as min-cost flow with one unit per vertex.

General graphs: odd cycles break Kuhn's search, because an alternating walk can reach the same vertex at both an even and an odd step. Edmonds' blossom algorithm fixes this by shrinking each odd cycle into a single vertex and continuing; it runs in O(V³).

Example of König failing: a triangle. The maximum matching is 1 edge, but you need 2 vertices to cover all 3 edges. In general graphs minimum vertex cover is NP-hard, so "V − matching" is no longer the maximum independent set.

code.title: Large-graph SCC: CSR arrays, trimming and forward-backward BFS
code.python:
n = 10
frm = [0, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 4]
to = [1, 2, 0, 3, 4, 5, 3, 5, 7, 6, 0, 9]

def csr(a, b):
    # CSR: neighbours of v are tgt[off[v] .. off[v+1]-1]; two flat int arrays, no objects
    off = [0] * (n + 1)
    for x in a:
        off[x + 1] += 1
    for v in range(n):
        off[v + 1] += off[v]
    pos = off[:]
    tgt = [0] * len(a)
    for i in range(len(a)):
        tgt[pos[a[i]]] = b[i]
        pos[a[i]] += 1
    return off, tgt

def reach(s, g):
    # BFS (no recursion) over nodes that have no SCC yet
    off, tgt = g
    seen = [False] * n
    seen[s] = True
    queue = [s]
    head = 0
    while head < len(queue):
        u = queue[head]
        head += 1
        for i in range(off[u], off[u + 1]):
            v = tgt[i]
            if not seen[v] and comp[v] < 0:
                seen[v] = True
                queue.append(v)
    return seen

fw, bw = csr(frm, to), csr(to, frm)
comp = [-1] * n
count = trimmed = 0
# trim: a node with no in-edges or no out-edges is an SCC by itself
for v in range(n):
    if fw[0][v] == fw[0][v + 1] or bw[0][v] == bw[0][v + 1]:
        comp[v] = count
        count += 1
        trimmed += 1
# forward-backward: SCC of the pivot = (reachable from it) AND (can reach it)
for p in range(n):
    if comp[p] >= 0:
        continue
    f, b = reach(p, fw), reach(p, bw)
    for v in range(n):
        if f[v] and b[v]:
            comp[v] = count
    count += 1
print("CSR offsets: [" + ", ".join(map(str, fw[0])) + "]")
print("CSR targets: [" + ", ".join(map(str, fw[1])) + "]")
print("trimmed single-node SCCs:", trimmed)
print("SCC id of each node: [" + ", ".join(map(str, comp)) + "]")
print("SCC count:", count)
# Two BFS per pivot: O((V + E) * number of SCCs) worst case, O(V + E) space; the BFS parts parallelise

followUps:
Because the result of a DFS depends on the exact order of visits: which vertex is entered next depends on everything that was visited before it. Two workers cannot explore two children of the same vertex at the same time, because what the first child's subtree swallows decides what is left for the second.

Example: edges 0 → 1, 0 → 2, 1 → 2. A sequential DFS visits 0, 1, 2, so 2 is a child of 1 and finishes before 1. If a second worker explores 0 → 2 in parallel, 2 becomes a child of 0 with different discovery and finish times, and Kosaraju's finish order or Tarjan's low values are no longer valid.

BFS has no such problem: all vertices of one level can be expanded at once and the levels come out the same. That is why large-scale SCC code is built from parallel reachability (forward-backward, trimming, colouring) instead of DFS.

Check the two properties that define a correct answer instead of trusting the run: every component is really strongly connected, and the graph of components has no cycle. Together they prove the labels are exactly right.

  • Acyclic condensation: build the component graph from edges whose ends have different labels and run Kahn's topological sort on it. Any leftover node means two components should have been merged. This is one pass over the edges.
  • Strongly connected inside: for a sample of components (and all the big ones), run a forward and a backward BFS from one member, staying inside the label; both must reach all members.
  • Sanity counts: sizes add up to V; compare the number of components and the size histogram with a previous run.
  • Small-scale test: run the same code on a subgraph that fits one machine and compare with Tarjan.

code.title: 2-SAT solved with SCCs of the implication graph

followUps:
Use two clauses: (a ∨ b) says at least one is true, and (¬a ∨ ¬b) says they are not both true. Together they mean a and b have different values (a XOR b).

Each clause gives two edges, so four implications go into the graph: ¬a → b, ¬b → a, a → ¬b and b → ¬a.

void addClause(int a, int b) {     // (a or b); lit ^ 1 = negation
  g[a ^ 1].add(b); g[b ^ 1].add(a);
}
addClause(a, b);           // at least one
addClause(a ^ 1, b ^ 1);   // not both

Check with a = true: the edge a → ¬b forces b = false, as wanted. Note that "exactly one of three or more" does not fit this way: the "at least one" part would be a clause with three literals, which is no longer 2-SAT.

Because a clause with three literals does not turn into simple "if this then that" edges. With two literals, (a ∨ b) means "if a is false then b must be true": one literal forces one literal, which is an edge. With three, (a ∨ b ∨ c) only says "if a is false then b or c is true". The conclusion is a choice, and a graph edge cannot hold a choice.

Without the implication graph the SCC test has nothing to work on, and you are back to trying combinations. Example: with ¬a known you still do not know whether to set b or c, and a wrong guess may only show up many clauses later.

This is a real boundary, not a missing trick: 2-SAT is solved in O(n + m), while 3-SAT is NP-complete, so no polynomial algorithm for it is known.

code.title: Iterative Tarjan SCC on a 200,000-node chain
code.python:
n = 200000
# chain 0 -> 1 -> ... -> n-1 plus one edge n-1 -> n/2: recursion would be 200000 deep
g = [[v + 1 if v + 1 < n else n // 2] for v in range(n)]
disc = [-1] * n
low = [0] * n
nxt = [0] * n
on_stack = [False] * n
call, st = [], []                    # our own call stack and Tarjan's stack
timer = count = largest = 0
for s in range(n):
    if disc[s] >= 0:
        continue
    call.append(s)
    while call:
        v = call[-1]
        if disc[v] < 0:              # first time we see v: the "enter" work
            disc[v] = low[v] = timer
            timer += 1
            st.append(v)
            on_stack[v] = True
        if nxt[v] < len(g[v]):       # nxt[v] remembers where the loop stopped
            w = g[v][nxt[v]]
            nxt[v] += 1
            if disc[w] < 0:
                call.append(w)       # "recursive call"
            elif on_stack[w]:
                low[v] = min(low[v], disc[w])
        else:                        # all edges done: the "return" work
            call.pop()
            if low[v] == disc[v]:
                size = 0
                while True:
                    w = st.pop()
                    on_stack[w] = False
                    size += 1
                    if w == v:
                        break
                count += 1
                largest = max(largest, size)
            if call:
                p = call[-1]
                low[p] = min(low[p], low[v])
print(f"nodes: {n}, edges: {n} (chain plus one back edge)")
print("SCC count:", count)
print("largest SCC:", largest)
# Time O(V + E), space O(V) on the heap - no deep recursion, so no stack overflow

followUps:
Keep your own stack of vertices and a "next edge" index per vertex; do the entry work the first time a vertex is on top, and the return work when it is popped.

  1. Top vertex not visited yet: set disc and low, push it on Tarjan's stack.
  2. It still has an edge: take it; push an unvisited neighbour, or update low from a neighbour that is on the stack.
  3. No edges left: pop it, pop its SCC if low == disc, and pass its low to the new top (its parent).
v = call.peek();
if (disc[v] < 0) { disc[v] = low[v] = timer++; st.push(v); on[v] = true; }
if (next[v] < g[v].size()) { w = g[v].get(next[v]++);
  if (disc[w] < 0) call.push(w); else if (on[w]) low[v] = min(low[v], disc[w]); }
else { call.pop(); if (low[v] == disc[v]) popScc(v);
  if (!call.isEmpty()) low[call.peek()] = min(low[call.peek()], low[v]); }

O(V + E) time, O(V) heap memory.

Everything built on BFS or on a simple loop is already safe; the DFS-based ones are the risk.

  • Naturally iterative: Edmonds-Karp (BFS for each path), the BFS levelling step of Dinic, Hopcroft-Karp's BFS phase, Hierholzer with an explicit stack, building the binary lifting table from a BFS order and answering LCA queries, Kahn's topological sort on the condensation, and forward-backward SCC with BFS.
  • Recursive by nature: Tarjan SCC, bridges and articulation points, Kosaraju's first pass, Kuhn's augmenting search, Dinic's blocking-flow DFS, and a DFS that fills depth and parent for LCA.

Example: on a 105-node chain, the depth table for LCA is fine if filled by BFS but overflows the stack if filled by a recursive DFS. Dinic's DFS only goes as deep as the S–T distance, so it is a problem only on long, thin networks.
